title: What is known about 1RB0RF_1LC---_1LF1LD_1RE0LD_0RC0RE_1LC1RA
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0RF_1LC---_1LF1LD_1RE0LD_0RC0RE_1LC1RA.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: Open, probviously halting. The run alternates between two kinds of sweep that multiply a count k of copies of 10 by about 3/2 per half-phase (the zigzag is proved in Lean). A short word w at the left end is a memory: the next w and the exact correction depend only on w and the parity of k, by a table read off simulation. The machine halts exactly when w reaches a pattern with four ones in a row together with the wrong parity of k. The orbit avoids it for 2,000,005 half-phases; with random parities it is reached after about 240 half-phases.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (B1); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 63,022 cells have been visited and 26,863 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: The zigzag that turns (10)<sup>k</sup> into ones
claims.text: For every j, x, y and every tape L on the left: L (10)^(x+2j) 1 1 E> 0 1 1^(2y+1) 0^inf reaches L (10)^x 1 1 E> 0 1 1^(2y+6j+1) 0^inf. Each round uses up two copies of 10 at the junction and adds six ones at the right end of the tape, the head sweeping over the whole block of ones and back.

claims.title: 34 half-phases, 7.6·10<sup>13</sup> steps, no halt
claims.text: With the macro simulator the run reaches step 7.6·1013. At the end of each half-phase the tape is a short word w followed by k copies of 10 or of 01, with k = 4, 10, 19, 35, 55, 86, 133, 203, 307, 464, 700, 1055, 1585, 2381, 3578, …, 7,950,370; the two words alternate.

claims.title: The exact half-phase map on (w, k)
claims.text: At a half-phase end the tape is w (10)^k F> (or w (01)^k A>). The next end is w′ (10)^k′ with k′ = (3k + c)/2, where w′ and c depend only on w and the parity of k. Each entry of the table is read off direct simulation for 12 values of k of that parity between 60 and 140 and is the same for all of them; the 50 entries the orbit uses so far give c ∈ {5, 7, 8, 9, 11, 14, 17}. Along the run from blank tape the table reproduces all 21 half-phases simulated directly (k up to 61,267) and the 34 of the macro simulator (k up to 7,950,370).

claims.title: 2,000,005 half-phases without a halt
claims.text: Run with the table, the orbit from blank tape makes 2,000,005 half-phases without meeting a halting entry; k then has 352,184 digits (about 10<sup>704,000</sup> machine steps; others report direct simulation to 1.1·10<sup>79</sup>). It visits only 42 word states, most often w = '', '1', '1000', '101', '11000' (each about half as often as the one before), and never one where the other parity of k would have halted. The shortest way to a halting entry needs 41 prescribed parities in a row, so a halt is expected only after about 2<sup>40</sup> half-phases (the estimate below), when k has about 10<sup>12</sup> bits: out of reach of this method.

claims.title: Where it halts: words with four ones in a row
claims.text: A half-phase halts (B reads 1 near the left end) only from a few (w, parity) pairs, all with 1111 in w: ('1111', odd), ('111101', odd), ('11111', even), … Among the 2,958 word states reachable from the start under some sequence of parities (|w| ≤ 18) there are 45 halting entries. The shortest way there takes 41 half-phases with prescribed parities: w counts up through '1', '1000', '101', '11000', '1101', '1000000', …, '1111000', '111101' and then needs an odd k.

claims.title: Probviously halting, after about 2<sup>40</sup> half-phases
claims.text: If the parities of k behave like fair coins, the word state is a Markov chain on these states, and the chance of a halt within 2<sup>e</sup> half-phases is 6·10<sup>-8</sup> for e = 16, 4·10<sup>-3</sup> for e = 32, 0.62 for e = 40 and 0.9996 for e = 43. So the machine halts with probability 1 in this model, but only after about 10<sup>12</sup> half-phases, when k has about 2·10<sup>11</sup> digits.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Given the table (sampled, not proved), exactly when the orbit of (w = '', k = 4) meets a halting entry, i.e. a word with four ones in a row and the wrong parity of k. That is a question about the parities of the ×3/2 sequence k, coupled to the word: Collatz-like.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB0LA_0RC0RB_1LD1LA_1LC1RE_1RF0RD_1LC--- up to renaming, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. The tape is a short word followed by k copies of 10 or 01; every half-phase multiplies k by about 3/2, and the parity of k edits the short word at the left end. This page shows the two sweeps (one proved in Lean), the half-phases, and what the question comes down to.

facts.text: No halt in the C simulator; 63,022 cells visited.
No halt, proved in Lean; the first 10,000 by the kernel alone.
The zigzag eating copies of 10, proved for every size.
No halt with the exact (sampled) map; k has 352,184 digits.
Half-phases before a halt if the parities of k are coin flips.

sections.heading: Multiplying by 3/2, over and over
html: The left end of the tape barely moves (33 cells left of the start); everything grows to the right. At the end of each half-phase the tape is a short word w at the left end followed by k copies of a two-cell word, 10 or 01, and the head is at the right end.

First the copies of 10 are eaten from the right: in each round the head, at the junction between the copies and a growing block of ones, uses up two copies and the block gains six ones, the head running over the whole block and back (proved in Lean for every size):

So k copies become about 3k ones. A second sweep then turns the block of ones into copies of 01 (or 10), one copy per two ones: about 3k/2 copies. Then it starts again, with the roles of the two words exchanged.

The memory word

Write the end of a half-phase as (w, k). The next one is (w′, (3k + c)/2), and w′ and c depend only on w and on whether k is even or odd. For instance from w = '' an even k gives w′ = '1', c = 8 and an odd k gives w′ = '', c = 11; from '1' an odd k gives '1000', c = 5. So w is a small automaton driven by the parities of k, a little like a counter: from the start, a lucky sequence of 41 parities walks it up to '111101', and from there an odd k halts the machine. The real orbit has done 20,000 half-phases with w staying among 25 short words.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape stopped growing in the second half of the run (bounded so far, or growing so slowly that no record fell in the last half). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.51).
After 109 steps the tape spans 63,022 cells (33 left of the start, 45,975 right), with a density of 1s of 0.426.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is the next thing to find.

sections.heading: A 3/2 map and a small memory
html: The count k follows k → (3k + 2c)/2 with a small c that depends on the parity of k and on the word w at the left end, and w itself is rewritten by each half-phase. This is the signature of a Collatz-like iteration: whether the halting transition (state B reading a 1, near the left end) is ever met depends on the parities of a sequence that grows by 3/2 at each step, which nobody knows how to control.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state. These are different runs: in the first 107 steps of each, no configuration of this machine's run occurs in the other, even up to a shift of the tape. So each of these holdouts is its own halting question, and settling one does not settle another.

summary: k copies of 10 -> (3k+c)/2 per half-phase, with a memory word w edited by the parity of k; halts when w gets 1111 with the wrong parity: probviously halting after ~2^40 half-phases.
family: Collatz-like x3/2 map with a memory word (probviously halting)
